narrative_purpose: Shows the splenic contraction as a physical event: an organ squeezing stored red cells into circulation seconds after submersion, for a real but modest gain.
subject: An anatomical cutaway of a diving torso seen from the front, semi-transparent, oriented head-up. Low on the left side sits a dark red elongated organ shown mid-contraction, its capsule visibly tightened and its outline smaller and more puckered than a relaxed organ would be. A dense stream of tiny glowing disc-shaped red cells is leaving it through a single vessel and joining a larger vessel that runs upward toward the heart, where the cells disperse into a brighter, denser crowd filling the central circulation. The vessels of the arms and the outer body wall are drawn narrow and dim by contrast.
scene: Dark water surrounding the torso, nothing else in frame, faint suspended particles.
camera: Front-on medium view of the torso from shoulders to hips, filling most of the frame.
light: Warm crimson glow from the contracting organ and the stream of cells, brighter crimson pooling at the heart, everything peripheral in deep indigo shadow with a faint cool teal rim from the water.
palette: Deep crimson and warm red for blood and organ, void indigo shadow, cool teal rim light, one small cyan accent.
style: Painterly naturalist anatomical plate, wet and organic, hand-painted texture.
detail_level: High detail on the puckered contracting capsule and the dense stream of individual cells; the torso outline soft and simplified.
composition: Organ low-left, vessel and cell stream rising diagonally to the heart at centre, open dark space in the upper-right and lower-left corners for overlay callouts.
consistency_notes: The organ reads as a soft contractile sac being squeezed, not a cut or wounded organ. The cells are small discs, many of them, clearly moving in one direction. no artificial graphics anywhere — direction is shown by the shape of the stream.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no graphs, no surgical or clinical look, no photographic or 3D-render look, no cartoon style
